transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-25
Time: 16:00 - 16:52 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Northshore Head of ML), Marcus King (Northshore SRE), Dr. Wei Huang (Northshore CTO)

Summary: Short intake to qualify dedicated/reserved capacity needs for Northshore's inference fleet. Focus on isolation (single-tenant requirement for PHI), warmpool prewarm behavior for morning spikes, and deterministic failure modes.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros — I'm Alex, AE. Priya is our solutions engineer. Could each of you say hi and your primary concern?
[00:12] Lena: Hi, Lena Ortiz — Head of ML. Our main thing is predictable p99 latency during our morning sync window. We run models for clinical note parsing, PHI, so isolation and audit logs are must-haves.
[00:24] Marcus: Marcus King, SRE. My worry is node failure during spike windows and how Redwood's reserved pool behaves — eviction, preemption, fallback. We want clear failure-mode semantics.
[00:34] Wei: Wei here — CTO. Compliance: SOC2, KMS integration, and data residency. Also cost — dedicated makes sense but we need burst economics.
[00:46] Priya: Thanks. We typically recommend a mix: reserved nodes for baseline throughput + warmpool for short spikes. We also support private deployment when customers want full VPC/on-prem control.
[00:58] Lena: Can you define warmpool? Is it prewarmed tensors in GPU memory or just idle nodes ready to schedule?
[01:08] Priya: Good question. Our warmpool is a set of preprovisioned nodes that we keep with model KV cache and a small number of prewarmed processes. It isn't full model-resident for every variant, but for common model+token lengths we keep KV caches and frequently used kernels hot — think soft-warm. That reduces first-token 99th by 200-300ms in our internal benchmarks for typical LLM sizes.
[01:33] Marcus: That 200-300ms sounds promising but what about a full cold start then? If a node is evicted or dies, how quickly can it be brought back and what is the variance?
[01:45] Priya: If a node is lost we have automated replacement to allocate a new reserved node; provisioning time varies by cloud/hardware but typically 2-6 minutes for full readiness. The warmpool can mask that if you have enough headroom — warmpool serves as short-term absorb. We can also pin model shards to dedicated disk to speed rehydrate.
[02:05] Lena: Our SLO is p99 < 600ms for text-parsing endpoints under production load. We saw spikes hitting 1.2s in our in-house tests.
[02:15] Alex: Understood. Is that measured across a mixture of sequence lengths? Any long-tail outliers?
[02:21] Lena: Mostly 256 token median, but we occasionally get 1024 tokens for some batch jobs. The morning spike is bursts of many short requests, though.
[02:30] Priya: That distribution matters. For many short requests we suggest a dedicated baseline with autoscale buffer plus warmpool at 10-20% of peak. On isolation: we offer single-tenant reserved nodes where the tenant owns the GPUs, which eliminates noisy neighbor risk and gives stronger compliance boundaries.
[02:51] Marcus: Single-tenant is a must for us. PHI and internal audit. How are logs retained and can we ship audit logs to our SIEM?
[02:59] Priya: Yes — we have audit logs, per-route token-level traces, and we can stream logs to customer SIEMs over secure forwarders. We support KMS/HSM key rotation with customer-managed keys for Private deployments; for Hosted Dedicated we offer bring-your-own-key integrations.
[03:20] Wei: What about failure modes — can Redwood simulate evacuation? We run chaos tests and need to understand blast radius.
[03:28] Priya: We can run failover drills. Our recommended pattern is: baseline reserved pool sized for steady-state plus warmpool for spikes. On node evacuation, routing moves traffic to warmpool or compatible model variants. If warmpool exhausted, we fallback to quantized variants or smaller-context models as a graceful degradation. We can document exact fallback chain and work with you on acceptable quality vs latency tradeoffs.
[03:58] Lena: How deterministic is fallback? We can't have silent quality regressions without notifying product.
[04:04] Alex: We integrate quality guards — regressions trigger alerts tied to eval prompt sets. We can gate automatic fallback behind canary thresholds if you want manual approval for quality-impacting fallbacks.
[04:18] Marcus: Now on capacity sizing — we hit regular daily 9-10am spikes for ~30 minutes. Baseline is ~12 GPU-utilized units, peaks transiently to 36 units. We want to avoid overcommitting. How do you bill for warmpool capacity?
[04:35] Priya: Billing model: reserved capacity is a committed monthly fee; warmpool is a paid-on-use buffer with prewarm standing charge + short-term usage for bursts. We typically show an example: commit to 12 GPUs reserved, warmpool of 8 GPUs with a small standing warm fee, and burst consumption billed at a slightly higher on-demand rate. We can send a T-shirt pricing spreadsheet.
[05:01] Marcus: Is there a hard cap on bursts? If 50% of customers spike concurrently will you throttle?
[05:08] Priya: We have routing policies. We can configure tenant priorities; you can get guaranteed throughput up to committed capacity and then warmpool and fallback. If the entire region is under stress, automatic fallback and throttling policies kick in — we can set per-tenant budgets and implement graceful reject responses.
[05:27] Lena: About prewarm content: can we prepopulate KV cache with embeddings for our most common prompts?
[05:34] Priya: You can provide representative prompt sets and we can precompute prefix caches. There's a tradeoff in memory; we typically prewarm hotspot tokens and common instruction prefixes. If you have a fixed set, we can do deeper prewarmed state.
[05:48] Marcus: For hardware, we use A100 equivalent. Any special kernel selection or quantization differences for those?
[05:56] Priya: We pick kernels per model and hardware — we compile to hardware-optimized kernels. For dedicated we support INT8/4 quantization paths if you want smaller models for fallback; for mission-critical model correctness you can keep FP16 on reserved nodes.
[06:12] Lena: Security questions — SAML SSO and RBAC for engineers and auditors. Can RBAC be integrated with our existing identity provider?
[06:20] Alex: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning supported. Role mapping can be done to your IdP. For private on-prem installs you control the IdP entirely.
[06:30] Marcus: Marcus to Priya — can we get an evacuation runbook example? We want concrete API calls to drain nodes, preempt jobs, and route to fallback.
[06:38] Priya: Absolutely; I'll attach a draft in the next-day followup. It will include drain node API, cache flush options, and recommended backlog shaping.
[06:49] Wei: What about multi-region fallback? We need data residency in EU for some customers. If the EU region is saturated, will routing send EU traffic to US?
[06:58] Priya: We never route outside a permitted region for a tenant that requires residency. We support region affinity. For global customers we recommend a cross-region reserved capacity plan with explicit failover permissions.
[07:14] Lena: One more: can Redwood run a short perf benchmark against our real prompts? We want p50/p95/p99 with and without warmpool.
[07:22] Priya: Yes. We can run a 48-hour warmpool benchmark using your prompt set and injected spike patterns. We'll collect token-level latency and tail distributions and send a benchmark report.
[07:33] Alex: Recap and timeline: Alex sends pricing + contract T&Cs, Priya scopes the benchmark and runbook, Marcus supplies historical utilization traces. We agreed to target the benchmark week of Feb 1.
[07:45] Marcus: I'll pull the traces and SRE runbook snippets. Expect them by Friday the 29th.
[07:51] Lena: Also send SOC2 report and KMS integration notes.
[07:56] Alex: Will do. Anything else?
[08:00] Wei: Cost sensitivity — if the warmpool costs are too high would you recommend a hybrid with some private on-prem reserved nodes?
[08:07] Priya: Yes, hybrid is common: keep the most latency-sensitive workloads on private/dedicated on-prem and route less-sensitive tasks to hosted dedicated. We'll show examples.
[08:18] Alex: Great. We'll follow up with the artifacts. Thanks all.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional word swaps, e.g., 'K-V cache' transcribed as 'K V cache' and 'warmpool' sometimes as 'hot pool'. Natural pauses and interruptions present.

Meeting close and explicit next steps recorded in metadata.
